usage_notes.narrative: Dunbar prescribes the dominant seventh chord as the primary vehicle for convergence, identifying it as 'the largest and most flexible of all the chord types' due to its tritone. Multiple scale colors (major, minor, augmented, dominant, diminished) are to be rotated over a single dominant seventh chord in varying orders -- 'many different scale color types on one chord (7th)' -- derived from listening to Coltrane and Lateef. The player may combine several scales together 'in several rotas varying their order' for richer harmonic color. Chapter 1, p. 4.

Dunbar prescribes expanding the plain dominant seventh into its alteration variants -- specifically 7b9, 7#5, 7#9, and 7b5 -- as direct applications of the tritone's flexibility. The book states: 'The 7th chord having the all important tritone host the largest and most flexible of all the chord types. (7th bs, 7b 9, 7th #5, 7th #9, 7th 9s).' Each variant is a legitimate convergence chord at the V position of any II-V cadence. Chapter 1, p. 4.

Dunbar explicitly names 7b9 as one of the load-bearing variants hosted by the dominant seventh's tritone: 'The 7th chord having the all important tritone host the largest and most flexible of all the chord types. (7th bs, 7b 9, 7th #5, 7th #9).' The 7b9 voicing is prescribed as a natural expansion of the basic V7 in the convergence system, particularly in II-V cadences and turnbacks where additional color is desired. Chapter 1, p. 4; Chapter 8, p. 69.

Dunbar prescribes altered dominants -- including 7#5 and 7#9 forms -- as direct outgrowths of the convergence system's tritone logic. The tritone within the dominant seventh is identified as the 'mysterious' central interval of the II-V cadence, and chromatic tones are used to resolve it: 'It is just a matter of using chromatic tones to resolve the tritone.' The 7#5 and 7#9 variants are named explicitly alongside 7b9 as members of the dominant seventh family eligible for convergence use. Chapter 1, p. 4; Chapter 8, p. 69.

Dunbar prescribes that any main chord in a tune may be approached by a preceding dominant seventh a tritone away: 'Whatever chord you are leading up to (main chord) is or can be usually preceded by a five chord with a tritone. This interval participates in this five or dominant-seventh chord as well as another seventh chord a flatted 5th from its root.' The Circle of Gravities (Chapter 8) maps these tritone relationships systematically and is the prescribed navigational tool for chord-on-chord motion. Chapter 8, p. 66.

Dunbar's convergence system was explicitly 'conceived at the II-V cadence,' and the II chord -- including the half-diminished (min7b5) quality appropriate to minor II-V progressions -- is a primary application target. Scale #15, described as 'half-diminished / half-whole-tone,' is specifically prescribed for convergence contexts involving half-diminished color: 'The scale has one half of its length yielding diminish color.' Scale #15's E natural leading tone is cited as resolving directly to F (the target tonal destination), making it the prescribed scale approach for minor ii function. Chapter 3, p. 32.

Dunbar prescribes two distinct diminished scale types as convergence vehicles, differentiated by interval structure. Scale #4 uses H-W symmetry (half-whole-half-whole) and Scale #5 uses W-H symmetry (whole-half-whole-half): 'This scale is a second type diminish scale. It has a W,H,W,H,W,H,W,H step symmetry. It permits ascending diminish color to a point of convergence.' Both are prescribed for bombarding a target tonal center with diminished color; the practitioner chooses between H-W and W-H depending on the approach direction and color desired. Chapter 2, pp. 21-22.

Dunbar prescribes Dorian mode as a direct convergence scale over the II (minor seventh) chord: 'This scale is simply a dorian mode of the F major.' Furthermore, G Jazz Melodic Minor -- which shares the same pitch content -- is prescribed as an interchangeable II-convergence substitute: 'the G Jazz melodic minor scale has the same notes as this scale so it may be used as a II convergence scale.' Both are valid because the final tetrachord resolves into the target key. Chapter 4, p. 50.

When a convergence scale contains a major 3rd that conflicts with a minor chord target, Dunbar prescribes redirecting the scale to embellish the fifth of the minor chord rather than its root: 'Scale #3 has a major 3rd already in it so it has to used as above to embellish the 5th of the F minor.' This conflict-redirection rule preserves the minor tonic's harmonic identity while still allowing major-color scales access to convergence function. Chapter 8, p. 70.

Before applying any convergence scale over a dominant seventh (or any target chord), Dunbar prescribes priming the ear first: 'Before playing each scale in this system, you should brainwash your ear with the tonality (F major in this case) with several cadences into the key.' This preparatory step is mandatory in the method -- the ear must already hear the destination before executing the approach. Coupled with sound projection ('project yourself sound wise to it already having your attention on it'), these two steps constitute the prescribed pre-execution ritual for any convergence scale. Chapter 2, pp. 18, 20.

Dunbar prescribes extracting every possible chord from every convergence scale and treating those chords as resolution material: 'Extract all possible chords from all scales for resolution purposes.' The governing rule is that 'Each chord represents a member chord sound of one of the modes of the scale it comes from.' Applied to dominant seventh contexts, this means the practitioner should harvest all modal-member chords from each of the 24 scales and use them as approach/resolution chords over V7. Chapter 2, pp. 17, 20.

Dunbar prescribes a universal voice-leading rule that applies to every scale used over any chord in the system, with the dominant seventh as the primary target: 'The last note of all the scales in this system are only a whole or half step away from the 1st, 3rd, or 5th or root of the desired tonal destination.' This rule functions as the validation criterion for whether a scale qualifies as a convergence scale -- any scale whose final note does not land within a whole or half step of a chord tone of the target is not admissible. Chapter 2, p. 22.

Dunbar prescribes Scale #16 -- a major scale with raised 4th (Lydian-like) -- as a convergence vehicle targeting major tonality. The scale 'begins on the 7th of the V chord of F major,' meaning it approaches the major tonic from the leading tone of the dominant, with the raised 4th equaling the major 3rd of the V chord. This construction is prescribed as a major-color convergence scale that satisfies the universal last-note resolution rule while contributing Lydian color to the approach. Chapter 3, p. 33.

Dunbar prescribes Scale #11 -- his personal descending scale built on an E-Bb tritone -- as a distinctive convergence vehicle for dominant seventh contexts. The scale is usable 'from any note within it,' and all scales including this one 'may be connected together in different orders for convergence into a tonal center.' Scale #11's tritone matches the tritone embedded in the V7 chord, making it a natural harmonic fit for approaching the tonal destination through the dominant. Chapter 3, pp. 28, 30.
